item.title: Bad News Travels Fast—Except to the Boss
item.description:
Leadership

Bad News Travels Fast—Except to the Boss

Why employee silence turns manageable issues into exhausting leadership crises.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • An open-door policy does not guarantee employees will bring bad news early.
  • How leaders respond to problems can determine whether employees speak up next time.
  • Delayed warnings can create bigger emergencies and more stress for leaders.
When bad news reaches leaders too late, manageable problems can become exhausting emergencies.
Source: Jeff Frey, used with permission

We’ve all heard the phrase “bad news travels fast.” True. Except, sometimes, to the boss.

By the time a problem reaches the person in charge, it may have been growing for weeks. Employees know. A partner is frustrated. The deadline is nearly here. Now the leader has an emergency that should have reached them long before.

In one of my research interviews, a nonprofit executive described discovering that her team was significantly behind in recruiting families for a program. They had been struggling for about three months. An important outside partner had already questioned the poor results in a meeting. She found out afterward.

Once she knew, she and the team quickly implemented ways to improve recruitment… but what frustrated her most wasn’t missing the target. It was learning about the problem too late to help.

“Was it a sense that they didn't want to bother me with that kind of detail?” she wondered out loud to me. It's a good question. But I think there's another, more uncomfortable one that she, and all of us who lead, should be asking:

“What have I done, or failed to do, that makes people hesitant to bring bad news to me?”

Why Bad News Gets Stuck

Leaders love to say, “My door is always open.” And sometimes it really is. But an open door doesn't tell an employee what will happen when they walk through it with information the boss doesn't want to hear.

Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety helps explain why. It's the shared belief that people can take interpersonal risks, including admitting mistakes and raising concerns, without being humiliated or punished (Edmondson, 1999).

Sure, employees don't always stay quiet out of fear. Some think they can fix the problem themselves. Some aren't sure it's serious enough. Others don't want to add to the boss's already full plate. But sometimes they've learned that the boss reacts in a way that turns bad news into worse news.

I have personally dealt with this. I once had a boss who took the “scorched earth” approach. Give him bad news, and he'd come in, blow up the situation, then leave us to put out the fires and reset. Not ideal.

Even being a great boss might matter less than you think. Detert and Burris studied more than 3,000 employees and found that managerial openness was more consistently related to speaking up than transformational leadership. Psychological safety helped explain the relationship (Detert & Burris, 2007). This suggests that being inspiring doesn't necessarily mean people feel safe bringing problems to you.

The Cost of Being the Last to Know

The real problem here for the leader is that silence feeds frustration. The longer the news is withheld, the bigger the problem can become, and the more frustrated the leader gets when it finally comes out. And if that frustration gets directed at the person who delivered the news? Well, they've just learned that next time, maybe they should wait even longer. More frustration. More silence. You get the idea.

Early on, there may be time to adjust a plan, offer help, or call a partner before trust is damaged. A month later, the same problem may force urgent decisions, damage relationships, and mean long evenings cleaning it up. The leader has fewer choices, and the ones left usually cost more relationally, financially, and often personally.

Ganster and Rosen's review of work stress and health describes how repeated workplace stressors can affect well-being through the cumulative burden of stress (Ganster & Rosen, 2013). One delayed report won't necessarily damage someone's health. But a steady stream of preventable crises adds strain to a job that already carries plenty.

Make It Easy to Tell You Early

The executive I interviewed already had a practical tool: a set of ground rules that amounted to “Tell me when…” After the incident, she revisited those rules with her team. She didn't need every detail of every program. She needed to know when something important was starting to slip.

For your organization, that might sound like this: Tell me when the numbers are heading the wrong way. Tell me when a partner is losing confidence. Tell me when you've tried something twice, and it isn't working. Don't wait until you have a polished explanation or a finished solution.

But rules won't help if your reaction teaches people to stay quiet. When someone brings a problem, notice your first response. Do you thank them for telling you, or immediately demand to know who's responsible? You can hold people accountable while still making it safe to raise a concern.

At your next team meeting, instead of “Is everything okay?” try “What are you noticing that we haven't talked about yet?” You may not love the answer. That's kind of the point.

Hear It While It's Still Small

Sustainable leadership isn't about making sure nothing goes wrong. It's about keeping manageable problems from becoming emergencies that consume your attention, energy, and health.

To lead sustainably, make bad news safe to deliver while it's still small. The sooner you know, the more you can do… and the less you may have to carry later.

item.title: Stop Shaming and Blaming the Sick and Injured
item.description:
Shame

Stop Shaming and Blaming the Sick and Injured

People generally do not choose to suffer pain or injury.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Many aspects of our culture inhibit the healing of the sick and injured by shaming and blaming them.
  • Unwell individuals exposed to these aspects come to shame and blame themselves.
  • This can inhibit them from taking compassionate care of themselves and seeking medical treatment.

Very few people choose to be sick or injured. Significant aspects of American cultural behavior can make these individuals feel guilty or ashamed. This can inhibit them from healing and seeking appropriate healthcare, often resulting in suboptimal and sometimes catastrophic outcomes. Individuals attempting to heal from illness or injury will do best to approach their healing with dignity and strength. They benefit from the support of their friends, family members, and providers in the form of compassion and encouragement.

The sources of shame and guilt toward the sick and injured are too numerous to fully describe here, but following are some very common sources.

Family Members and Friends

Those closest to the unwell often bear the burden of taking care of them and often have to make significant sacrifices. For example, they may have to forgo important or pleasurable activities to be available to their ailing loved one. There may be significant loss of income if the loved one is employed and does not have sick leave as a benefit.

Sustained illness or injury is often associated with feelings of resentment as the sacrifices continue. In some cases, caretaker burnout results. Even the most compassionate caretakers struggle to suppress these feelings over time. Most unwell individuals already feel inadequate and burdensome to others and are stung by these expressions.

Workplace

Many employment arrangements do not offer paid sick time. This encourages employees to work even when they are not well. It discourages them from seeking medical care if it interferes with their work schedule, which for 9-to-5 employees, is almost always. These employees are effectively fined for resting or seeking medical care, which is necessary for healing and recuperation.

Source: lu94007/Pixabay

Many workplaces reward employees for not taking sick time. They often pay them for unused days at the end of the year. This leaves those who need to take those days feeling guilty and ashamed for being ill.

Co-workers often are charged with “covering” for those out sick. They often feel like they are doing their job as well as someone else’s without additional compensation. This can be expressed actively by complaining about the burden, or passively by not doing the job adequately or completely. Unwell employees are then punished when they return to work by having to remedy problems created in their absence.

Doctors

The demand for physicians is greater than the supply. Doctors are often overworked. They are required to see as many patients as they can and often have to be on call when they are not seeing patients. This results in doctors often making their patients wait for scheduled appointments. It is common for patients to wait in doctors' waiting rooms or hospitals for over an hour, and sometimes for several hours, for scheduled and emergency visits.

Often, when the doctor finally does show up, they are often rushed and exhausted, making patients feel like they are burdensome. The lack of enough doctors often means that those requiring expedient care must see "physician extenders" (i.e., physician's assistants or nurse practitioners) rather than their doctor, also adding to the sense of being a burden or unworthy due to their unwellness.

These very common experiences leave the sick and injured feeling like they have to beg for standard medical care. In some cases, they are humiliated for feeling so needy.

Medical Insurance

When presenting for medical care, most sick and injured patients are required to sign documents promising to pay for medical care if their insurance company does not. Many sick and injured people cannot afford to pay for uncovered medical services. Some cannot afford the “copays” that many insurers levy on their subscribers. Feelings of humiliation are common when individuals suffering medically are turned away for lack of funds.

It is very common for medical insurers to seem to discourage medical care and encourage feelings of guilt and shame when they deny claims. This is often done with an audit or “utilization review,” after which patients are notified that they are not sick enough for the care they seek. This is tantamount to accusing them of committing fraud for seeking medical care.

General Population

Most individuals are uncomfortable with the idea that people can get sick or injured through no fault of their own. For example, they want to believe that if they never smoke cigarettes, they will never get lung cancer. If they maintain a healthy body weight, they will not get heart disease. These are good life choices, but to support this ideology they often ask questions that are hurtful to the unwell. Here are a few examples.

When people are diagnosed with lung cancer, they are asked, “Did you smoke?”

When people are diagnosed with skin cancer, they are asked, “Do you tan?”

When people are infected with a virus, they are asked, “Are you run down?”

When people are in automobile accidents, they are asked, “Were you drinking?”

In each of these common examples, it is implied that the person who is sick or injured might have avoided the pain if they were more diligent. While this might be an unintended consequence, it makes the unwell feel worse.

Self-Induced Guilt and Shame

With all of the above influences suggesting directly or indirectly that unwell individuals are that way by choice or weakness, it is not surprising that many individuals get angry with themselves when they get sick or injured. They go to work when they are sick. They avoid seeking medical care as long as possible. This can make them sicker.

Social and systemic reform is highly desirable. Unwell individuals should be treated with compassion by all. Everyone eventually gets sick or injured.

You cannot control what others think and say, but you can control how you cope with unwellness. Your healing and recovery will benefit from self-compassion. When you are sick or injured, your wellness becomes the number one priority in your life. Pursuing rest and treatment when you are unwell is championing your survival. This is strong and honorable and nothing that anyone should feel guilty or ashamed about.

item.title: Efforts to End Suffering by Captive Animals Help Them and Us
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Efforts to End Suffering by Captive Animals Help Them and Us

Declines in elephant rides and the development of sea sanctuaries are wins for all.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Captive elephants and cetaceans show neurotic, stereotypic behaviors from psychological trauma.
  • Tourist demand for elephant rides at Amer Fort dropped 70% in seven years amid welfare concerns.
  • As more people become concerned with animal well-being, tangible benefits for the animals emerge.

Co-written by Marc Bekoff, Ph.D., and science writer Shubhobroto Ghosh

The recent announcement of the decline in demand for elephant rides in Amer Fort in Jaipur in Rajasthan, India, and recent debates and controversy surrounding the plight of beluga whales at Marineland Niagara in Canada took me back to a topic that I addressed in a previous post, regarding the physical harms suffered by large captive mammals, including cetaceans and elephants. These latest developments add to the growing concern that visitors to venues that house captive animals, especially large mammals like cetaceans and elephants, are becoming increasingly aware that these animals suffer both physically and psychologically and that it is inappropriate and unethical to incarcerate them in captive facilities for human entertainment.

The decline of elephant rides

Ample research shows that elephants are extremely intelligent sentient animals. The recent observation of a female carrying a corpse that wasn't her own—referred to as being "an intimate moment, almost spiritual"—went global and clearly suggests the depth of their emotional lives.

Unfortunately, elephants continue to be abused in many sorts of entertainment venues, including zoos, circuses, and tourist camps. However, recent information released by government agencies in Rajasthan, India, reveals that there has been a decline of around 70 percent in tourist demand for elephant rides at Amer Fort over the past seven years. According to a news report, “The popularity of elephant safaris at the historic Amer Fort has declined sharply, with the number of tourists opting for elephant rides falling by around 70 per cent in seven years, according to official records. The figure rose to 9,560 in 2021-22, 54,514 in 2022-23, 79,090 in 2023-24 and 67,018 in 2024-25 before declining again to 48,474 in 2025-26.”

Captive elephants at Hathi Gaon in Jaipur in Rajasthan, India.
Source: Shubhobroto Ghosh

The campaign to highlight the physical and psychological suffering of captive elephants at Amer Fort goes back more than two decades, with organizations like World Animal Protection providing extensive investigative coverage of the emotional suffering of these animals in captivity. Ghosh has observed that the Amer Fort elephants—due to a lack of stimulation that is characteristic of their wild lives, including family bonding, play, walking long distances, natural environment ambience, interaction with other species, swimming, and adequate rest—exhibit severe abnormal behavioral stereotypies, including pacing and rocking back and forth, in the conditions in which they are held at Amer Fort and Hathi Gaon in Jaipur.

Forced to climb a steep, cobbled, sharp slope to the top of the fort, these elephants also endure injuries on the soles of their feet, and there have been several instances of their frustrations leading them to fight with each other and attack tourists, making this a hazardous, potentially lethal activity.

Numerous studies, conducted on both sides of the Atlantic and in Thailand and India, show that elephants in captivity suffer severely from the restrictive effects of captivity. Neurotic behavior has been observed in captive elephants. In every single facility, elephants display signs of stereotypies when their behavioral needs are not adequately addressed. This was pronounced in Delhi's last privately kept elephant, Laxmi, in Yamuna Bank. The decline in the demand for tourist rides is a welcome development for organizations like World Animal Protection, which has been spearheading the campaign to end elephant rides all over the world, and a sign of public enlightenment that wildlife entertainers are having to reckon with.

The fate of Canada's beluga whales

There is an ongoing controversy surrounding the fate of 30 or so beluga whales who were being held in Marineland Niagara in Canada. When Marineland closed and declared bankruptcy in 2024, the fate of their animals became unclear, particularly the beluga whales and four bottlenose dolphins kept there. Kiska, the site's lone killer whale, had died there in 2023, and the Marineland operator threatened to euthanize the others unless animal protection groups offered alternative homes.

Ghosh has seen these beluga whales, bottlenose dolphins, and Kiska. They were showing signs of abnormal behavior, including stereotypic repetitive behaviors. One beluga whale in Marineland was notorious for head bobbing. Scientists like Lori Marino and Ingrid Visser have demonstrated that captive cetaceans are psychologically traumatized and show signs of being neurotic. The possibility of the Marineland Niagara animals being sent to commercial captive venues in China raised genuine concerns for their welfare, and the recent deaths of some of the translocated belugas in commercial aquariums in the United States and Spain gained the attention of animal welfare and animal rights activists.

Fortunately, the development of cetacean sea sanctuaries may help to relocate some captive dolphins and beluga and killer whales, and there are elephant sanctuaries where they can live out their lives free from harm, without being subject to harsh treatment.

Research shows wildlife belongs in the wild

Living in captivity can have serious negative physical and psychological impacts on nonhumans and humans. The developments in India and Canada with regard to elephants and beluga whales indicate that these animals and others are best left free to live species-typical natural lives. Jane Goodall was of the firm conviction that animals like elephants and cetaceans should not be kept in captivity because their physical and psychological needs could not be met. Wildlife belongs in the wild.

Some people defend keeping animals in captivity, arguing that it helps conserve endangered species or offers educational benefits for visitors to zoos and aquariums. These justifications are questionable, especially for large mammals, and even if there are some examples where captive animals seem to be used to support conservation and education, they are few and far between. But as work by many scientists shows, caging large mammals and putting them on display is undeniably cruel because it causes brain damage and a host of associated behavioral anomalies.

Public perceptions of captivity are slowly changing, and there is increasing concern about the treatment and well-being of animals in zoos and aquariums. Witness the strong reaction to the award-winning documentary Blackfish and other exposés of what goes on behind the scenes.

Where animals cannot be freed, there are well-designed alternatives to being forced to live in substandard conditions. Transitions from abusive venues to well-designed sanctuaries may turn out to be the saving grace for improving the well-being of large mammals and many other animals.

What helps them can also help us. It is important to recognize that these and other successes will most likely also benefit people suffering from compassion and empathy fatigue and keep them going by reducing the costs of caring. This is a win-win for all. What could be better?

item.title: Envisioning Life Beyond Divorce
item.description:
Divorce

Envisioning Life Beyond Divorce

How envisioning your future can bring clarity and purpose to divorce.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Envisioning post-divorce life leads to better decisions and less conflict during divorce.
  • Success in divorce is unique; it depends on individual goals and visions for the future.
  • Self-compassion, not just optimism, predicts better emotional recovery after divorce.

In my practice as a divorce attorney, the first meeting with a new client almost always centers on the past: what went wrong, who said what, how long the marriage has been struggling. That is natural. But the most important question I ask in that first meeting is about the future: When your divorce is final, what do you want your life to look like?

Many clients have no answer. Some have never even allowed themselves to consider the question. Yet, the answer shapes nearly every decision that follows. Clients who can answer it tend to move through the process with more clarity and less conflict and have fewer regrets.

It’s extremely difficult to develop a successful strategy for the divorce process if you don’t know where you want to be at the end of the process. Success looks different depending upon the individual. For some, success is getting as big a share of the marital assets or as much support as possible. For others, it may be preserving the parenting relationship with the other parent. Success is surely not a one-size-fits-all proposition.

Divorce is one of the most stressful experiences a person can face. On the widely cited Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale, divorce ranks second only to the death of a spouse among major life events. And marital separation ranks third. Divorce rarely involves a single change. It often represents fundamental changes at the core of a person’s life. And they can all happen at once: a new household, new parenting schedule, new finances and financial responsibilities, and sometimes a new social circle.

Divorce can also unsettle a person's sense of identity. After years of marriage, "I" and "we" become deeply intertwined. Some clients say: "I don't know who I am if I'm not his/her spouse," “My whole social life has been plans with other couples. I don’t have any single friends anymore,” or “I don't know what my weekends look like without the kids." That uncertainty is normal. In my experience, it is also temporary.

What I see in clients who thrive

Over the years, I have watched many clients build full, satisfying lives after divorce. The distress of the early months is real, but it is rarely permanent. What distinguishes the clients who move forward most confidently is not their wealth, the length of their marriage, or even how contentious their case is. It is whether they begin, at some point in the process, to picture the life they want to build.

Those clients start to see themselves not only in conflict with a spouse or co-parent but as the author of what comes next. They make decisions from a sense of purpose rather than from fear or anger. They also tend to be patient with themselves. Research supports this: A University of Arizona study found that divorcing adults who approached their separation with self-compassion showed better emotional recovery in the months that followed, independent of self-esteem or optimism.

What many people don’t realize is that a divorce is a series of decisions about the future. Where will you live? How will you and your co-parent divide time with the children? How will you support yourself? Which assets matter to you, and why? A settlement agreement or court order will govern many of the questions for years, sometimes decades.

When a person has no vision of the future, those decisions can be made by default or be driven by emotions unrelated to that person’s best interests. Some clients fight hard for the marital home because giving it up feels like losing, only to discover later that it takes more resources than necessary to maintain and no longer want to live there. Others concede too quickly simply to end the conflict but trade their long-term security for short-term relief. In both cases, they make their decision based upon the marital relationship or their situation at that moment, instead of the life that comes after it.

A client who has taken time to envision the future can measure each decision against one clear question: Does this move me toward the life I want? That question often lowers the temperature of a negotiation, too. When both spouses focus on what they need going forward rather than on what went wrong, settlement becomes far more achievable.

Practical steps toward the next chapter

  • Separate grief from strategy. Anger, sadness, and fear are normal and deserve attention, ideally with the support of a therapist. But they should not make legal and financial decisions on your behalf. When a decision feels both urgent and emotional, pause.
  • Understand your finances. Many people, especially those whose spouse managed the money, feel anxious about finances. Learn your budget, your assets, and your obligations. Financial clarity reduces fear and makes realistic planning possible. In many situations, enlisting the assistance of a financial advisor can be helpful.
  • Be patient with yourself. Harsh self-criticism rarely leads to good decisions. Treat yourself as you would a good friend going through the same experience.
  • Reclaim pieces of your identity. Reconnect with friends, interests, and routines that belong to you alone. Small, independent activities help restore a sense of self.
  • Picture an ordinary day. Rather than setting lofty goals, imagine a normal Tuesday two or three years from now. Where do you wake up? What does your work look like? How do you spend time with your children? Concrete images are more useful than abstractions.
  • Build the right team. A therapist, a financial advisor, and an attorney each play a distinct role. Therapists can be especially helpful by encouraging separating clients to articulate their goals early and to share those goals with their legal and financial advisors before major decisions are made. Therapists can also be helpful having clients recognize what decisions are being driven by emotion instead of self-interest.

Looking ahead

No one should be expected to have the next chapter fully written on the day they start the divorce process. But the clients I see navigate divorce most successfully are those who allow themselves to imagine what comes next. That vision gives the entire process a direction. My role as a divorce attorney is to focus on this chapter so that my clients can look ahead to the next. The more clearly they can see that next chapter, the better equipped we are to build toward it together.
